lessons.title: ഫ (pha) — one character, met with the word that needs it
lessons.gloss: the single character ഫ — the breathed partner of പ, arriving with the word that needs it

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ഫ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: പ — say its sound.
One character this time. One only. It arrives with the word on the next page.
ഫ — pha.
It is the breathed partner of പ. Begin with the same lip closure, then let a puff of air follow the release: പ pa, ഫ pha.
Malayalam pairs stops this way — a plain one and a breathed one beside it. This one has not appeared in a headword yet; it arrives for the borrowed word on the next page.

blocks.title: Writing: ഫ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ഫ (pha) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these two, and say which one carries the breath
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these two, and say which one carries the breath]

segments.text: പ, ഫ (pha).

segments.instruction: ഫ three times, saying pha as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ഫ three times, saying *pha* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: pa, then pha — the same lips, one with a puff of air
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *pa*, then *pha* — the same lips, one with a puff of air]

segments.text: Which character is this — ഫ? What sound does it carry? (pha.) Which letter is it the breathed partner of? (പ.)

lessons.title: ഫോൺ (phōṇ) — a telephone
lessons.gloss: a telephone — an English borrowing whose first and last letters are now familiar

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script Lens: three pieces until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Think of the thing you would pick up to reach somebody far away.
You are about to find you can nearly say it already.
ഫോൺ (phōṇ) — a telephone.
Say it out loud and you will hear English. It is phone, borrowed whole, with the ending settled into Malayalam sounds: the n at the close is made with the tongue curled back, not at the teeth.
Read it from left to right:

utterances: ഫ, pha, the breathed partner of പ.
ൺ, final retroflex ṇ, with no following vowel.

segments.text: The first letter arrived on the page before this one. The last is the chillu you met inside അരുൺ near the beginning of the book. Together they let the borrowed English word settle into Malayalam spelling: ഫ (pha) + ോ + ൺ = ഫോൺ (phōṇ).

segments.instruction: ഫോൺ (phōṇ), with the tongue curled back at the end
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **ഫോൺ**, with the tongue curled back at the end]

segments.instruction: which language the word came from
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which language the word came from]

segments.instruction: ഫ (pha), ോ, ൺ, then the whole word

segments.text: A telephone? (ഫോൺ, phōṇ.) Where does the word come from? (English.) Which character closes it? (ൺ, final retroflex ṇ.)

lessons.title: കത്ത് (kattŭ) — a letter
lessons.gloss: a letter — the written kind, built from a doubling you have read since the school chapter

segments.text: Read and say the word for a telephone: ഫോൺ (phōṇ).
Now think of the older way of reaching somebody who is far off.
കത്ത് (kattŭ) — a letter, the kind you write and send.

Every piece of this word is one you can already read. The doubled ത്ത in the middle is the cluster you took apart in the school words, and the half-u at the end is the one you close dozens of words with.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a shape that hides inside a word you know

segments.text: You have read these characters before, sitting inside another word.
Cover the first character of അകത്ത് and what is left looks exactly like കത്ത് (kattŭ). The two words are not related, and the resemblance is worth meeting once so it cannot mislead you later.

You were told how to read that pair when you learned it: read the ends and not the fronts — അകത്ത് and പുറത്ത് end alike and differ at the front, which is where their meaning sits. കത്ത് (kattŭ) is a whole word rather than one of that pair, so the advice that sorts inside from outside is the same advice that keeps this one separate from both.

segments.instruction: at അകത്ത് and കത്ത് (kattŭ), and say which one means inside
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **അകത്ത്** and **കത്ത്**, and say which one means *inside*]

segments.instruction: a letter, and a telephone, one after the other
segments.source: [YOU SAY: a letter, and a telephone, one after the other]

segments.text: A letter? (കത്ത് (kattŭ).) Does it have anything to do with അകത്ത്? (No — the shapes overlap and the words do not.) A telephone? (ഫോൺ (phōṇ).)

lessons.title: തപാൽ (tapāl) — the post
lessons.gloss: the post — what carries the letter, and the word on the red box

segments.text: Say the word for a letter.
Then ask yourself what carries it.
തപാൽ (tapāl) — the post: the service, and the word printed on the box you drop a letter into.

utterances: തപാൽ (tapāl), the thing that carries it.

segments.text: The ending is one you can already read. ൽ is the chillu you have met closing other words — a bare l with no vowel after it.

segments.instruction: the letter and the post, in that order
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the letter and the post, in that order]

segments.instruction: at തപാൽ (tapāl) and name the character that closes it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **തപാൽ** and name the character that closes it]

segments.text: The post? (തപാൽ (tapāl).) The thing you put in it? (കത്ത് (kattŭ).) What closes തപാൽ (tapāl)? (The chillu ൽ.)

lessons.title: ഇമെയിൽ — ഇന്റർനെറ്റ് (imeyil — inṟarneṟṟŭ)
lessons.gloss: e-mail and the internet, and what you already own for saying an address out loud

segments.text: Say the post, and the thing it carries.
Then say the mark that ends a written sentence.
ഇമെയിൽ (imeyil) — e-mail.
ഇന്റർനെറ്റ് (inṟarneṟṟŭ) — the internet.
Both are English, borrowed whole and spelled in Malayalam letters, and both end the way you would expect: ഇമെയിൽ on the chillu ൽ you closed തപാൽ (tapāl) with, ഇന്റർനെറ്റ് on the half-u.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: you can already say an address out loud

segments.text: An examiner may ask you to say an e-mail address, and the pieces are in hand: the letters, and the full stop you were taught with the other marks. A Malayalam speaker reading an address aloud names that mark exactly where it sits.

The mark before the domain is a different matter. This book has not given you a Malayalam name for it, for the same reason it gave you no Malayalam names for the punctuation marks: those names exist and are not written down here until they can be given with a source. What you can do already is spell the letters and place the stop.

segments.instruction: which of the two carries the other
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two carries the other]

segments.instruction: the mark you name aloud when reading an address
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the mark you name aloud when reading an address]

segments.text: E-mail? (ഇമെയിൽ.) The internet? (ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്.) Which older pair do those two mirror? (തപാൽ (tapāl) carrying കത്ത് (kattŭ).)

lessons.title: (phone, letter, post, e-mail, internet) (sandesham enna oormma) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of five ways to reach somebody and the new letter that opens the first

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say telephone, letter and the post.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two ways of reaching somebody, a century apart

utterances: കത്ത് (kattŭ) carried by തപാൽ (tapāl), the older pair.
ഇമെയിൽ carried by ഇന്റർനെറ്റ്, the newer one.

segments.text: The newer pair is borrowed and the older one is not, which is the ordinary way a language takes in a new thing: the object arrives with its name attached. What is worth noticing is that the shape of the pair did not change — a thing written, and a service that carries it.
All five are words you can now read. The telephone added ഫ (pha), the breathed partner of പ, and reused the final ൺ from the opening chapters. The other four were already inside your script range.
You can now name the telephone, write and send a letter, and say an address aloud as far as the stop.
